newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Royal Bank powers higher on bid talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Royal Bank powers higher on bid talk.

text.p: Shares in Royal Bank of Scotland Plc rocketed in a surging UK bank sector on Friday, as an outbreak of bid speculation sparked fresh investment demand for a sector that has already risen sharply this year.

A Royal Bank spokeswoman dismissed the surge in the bank's shares as "just market speculation," while dealers said talk of a bid from HSBC Holdings Plc dated back as far as its failed bid for the Royal Bank in 1981.

Yet Royal Bank shares had leapt 55p or 8.5 percent to 658 by midmorning, the biggest gainer in the FTSE 100 by far and helping drive the blue chip index to the latest of a series of record highs, though they had fallen back to 642-1/2p by early afternoon.

HSBC shares were up 59-1/2p at 18.54-1/2 pounds, after earlier touching a record 18.65. A spokeswoman for the Anglo-Hong Kong banking group, which owns Midland Bank in Britain, also declined comment on what she said was no more than market rumour.
"Royal Bank gets linked with us two or three times every year," she added.
Other bank stocks also leapt, with Abbey National Plc, previously seen as a possible bid target as the sector consolidates, was up 20p at 904-1/2, after earlier reaching a record 915p.

Barclays Plc was up 42-1/2p at 12.51-1/2 pounds, Lloyds TSB Group Plc was up 11-1/2 at 614, Bank of Scotland Plc firmed 5p to 415, National Westminster Bank Plc gained 10p to 795 and Standard Chartered Plc rose 39p to 10.19-1/2 stg.

Recently-floated Alliance & Leicester Plc, expected to join the FTSE 100 index next month, also set the latest in a series of post-floation highs. It was up 5-1/2 at 632 by 1330 GMT, after earlier rising as high at 657p.
A report in the Financial Times helped ignite the sector's latest run, saying that the Royal Bank "would make an obvious target" for HSBC.

Yet dealers said much of Friday's surge in bank shares as a whole reflected continued attempts by investment funds to increase their holdings in the sector, ahead of the flotation of the Halifax Building Society -- the UK's biggest mortgage lender -- next month.

"The point is that Halifax is going to have a market capitalisation of say 12 billion pounds, yet no institution is going to own a single share," said the head of equity trading at one top U.S. investment bank.
"Automatically it means everyone is going to be underweight the sector and that is creating a dramatic technical squeeze."
But he said the bank sector, which has massively outperformed the rest of the British equity market in recent months, could see its bubble burst once the Halifax float was over.

"What we are seeing could be the sector's final flourish ahead of the Halifax issue," the head of trading said. "We are finding it difficult to justify buying some of these stocks at these sort of prices."
